column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
Left out the 1813 Triumvirate and the constitution commission, both already in the description.

The article does not say the duchy returned to direct papal rule in 1545 (the description's claim); it says she sold the duchy to Paul III in 1539 for 78,000 scudi. Left the 1545 date and the word 'seized' to the description.

The article contradicts itself on the budget (one third votable vs 75% non-votable), on Annie Besant (accepted the act vs called the reforms unworthy) and on who formed the Swaraj Party; left these out or followed the more specific statement. It also says the reserved list stayed with the Viceroy in one place and with the governor in another; the description has the governor. The Rs 3,000 franchise figure looked doubtful and was left out.
The article spells the saint Gwénnolé; the description has Guénolé. Death and legacy is used because the Life of Saint Winwaloe gives his death at the beginning of the 6th century.

The article says he reorganised the ducal library; the description says he founded the Palatine Library. Left the library out. The article gives no year for his dismissal, only his flight from Colorno on 19 November 1771.
The article places the Gullah from North Carolina to Florida; the description has the Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia. Did not give the wider range.

The article gives his nickname as the Quarrelsome or Bellicosus; the description has the Warlike. Left the English name out. The description dates the division to 1599; the article gives no year for it. Left the year out.
The article dates his succession to about 1053; the description gives 1053. Used 1053 only through the Arques episode.

The article says Guzgan's boundaries bear no relation to the modern Jowzjan and Faryab provinces; the description says it roughly matched them. Did not compare it with the provinces at all. The article does not date the start of Farighunid rule or the dedication of the Hudud al-Alam; left both to the description.

The article gives him the title Maharana; the description says rana. Left the title out. The article calls Hammir's grandfather both Rana Laksha and Lakshman Singh, Thakur of Sisoda; used Lakshman Singh.
The description says the pair were probably both male; the article says DNA confirmed it. Wrote that Selinsky and Monge concluded both were male, without 'confirmed'.

The article says he died in 741 and ruled from around 700 until his death, and places the fruit of Boniface's mission and the founding of the diocese of Erfurt (742) in his reign; the description dates him fl. c. 704-717 and says the duchy then passed under direct Frankish control. Left out the death year, Boniface and Erfurt. Two sections only: the article has little more.

The article says in one place that Helian Chang, not Ding, was made Duke of Pingyuan in 414 (a slip); left the title out. It dates the empress's capture to 430 in one section and around the new year of 431 in another; left the date out.
The article says he was bishop of Worms from 1524 to 1552; the description says he was 'later' bishop of Worms. Left the start of his Worms tenure out.

The article dates his accession to 1017 but also says he had let Sablé become independent by 1015; the description says about 1015. Left the year of accession out. The article gives his death as 13 April 1035; the description has c. 1035, so the exact date was left out. The article explains the nickname by his constant resistance to Angevin intrusions; the description by night raids. Left the explanation out.

The article gives the storage capacity as 84,016 cubic metres, which looks wrong for a city reservoir; left it out. Left out the article's superlatives for the boardwalk and aviary (longest in India, largest in the world).
The article gives no launch year; the entry's 1655 is not repeated or contradicted. The article calls the capture site the Medway raid without naming Chatham; neither is restated.

The article places the massif in north-eastern Algeria, the entry in north-central Algeria; the region is not named in the text. The article's sentence on the pilgrimage mountain names a summit of 1,659 m without a clear name (Djebel Guetiane is mentioned in a garbled sentence); left vague.

The article's lead says Ujinao 'carried on as a small daimyo in the Edo period', which contradicts his death in 1591 given in the same article and the entry; left out. The article says Kai is 'currently Gunma Prefecture'; left out. The article gives his death as 19 December 1591; only the year is used. The entry's 'fifth head' is not restated.
The article dates the Kirwin Chief reprint 21 March 1874 in one place and 26 March 1874 in another; only the month is given.

The article says Mound City has 25 mounds in one section and 23 in another; no count is given. The article names the landowner behind the culture's name as M. Cloud Hopewell in one place and Mordecai Hopewell in another; no first name is given. The park is said to have four sites in the lead and six units in the Location section; no count is given.

The article says his birth year is not known (the entry gives 503); no birth year is given. The entry says he defected after Gao Huan's death in 547; the article says he rebelled in spring 547 believing Gao Huan dead or near death. The text gives only 'spring 547' without tying it to the death. The article tells the drowning of his two sons twice in slightly different ways; it is told once. The article dates his death c. 26 May 552.

The entry dates the acquisition of Auvergne and Boulogne to the late 14th century (Bertrand IV's marriage to Marie I of Auvergne in 1389); the article adds that their son succeeded as count in 1437. Not restated. Left out: the Bouillon succession lawsuits and the Lauraguais claimants.
SKIPPED: too little: the article has under 250 words of substance and repeats much of the entry
SKIPPED: too little: the article has under 250 words of substance; it also dates the missal 1407 or later against the entry's 1403-1404

The article gives her birth as 'likely around 1240 or 1245'; the entry's c. 1245 is not restated. The article's account of the Jiaoche (a ginning machine that 'could spin out three yarns simultaneously by stepping') is confused; the three-spindle machine is in the entry and is not restated.
The entry's campaign against Gruffudd ap Cynan is not in the article and is not restated.

The article dates the capital from 1122 to 1153; the entry has Aguda ruling from there after proclaiming the dynasty in 1115. The start year is left out. The entry names the new capital Zhongdu, the article Yanjing (present-day Beijing); Yanjing is used.

The entry says Hulwan declined after the Mongol period; the article says it never recovered its prosperity after its destruction in 1046-1049. The decline is not dated in the text. Left out the 'Firuz Qubadh' Arabic forms for length.
The article's remark that Hungary 'currently' has a unicameral system is left out.

The article says he was born between 700 and 704; the entry gives 704. No birth year is given. The article's claim that Tibet was then ruled by Songtsen Gampo is anachronistic and is left out; so is its placing of Hyecho in the Three Kingdoms period. The entry says he spent the rest of his life in China translating texts; the article does not cover this and it is not restated.
The article dates his death c. 2380 BC; the entry gives the 24th century BCE, which agrees. Only the century is implied.
The article gives his birth year as 1400; the entry gives only his death in 1464.

The article dates the earliest settlements both to 900 BCE and to before 6000 BC; neither is given. The article calls Ojukwu 'Nigerian General'; only his name is given. Left out the 1966 coups and the French support quotation for length.
The article says he inherited the headship in 1558 when his father retired, and later that he succeeded his father after Okehazama in 1560; no date is given for his becoming head.

The entry says Le Hoan sacked Indrapura in 982; the article says he sacked a city in northern Champa (Quang Binh) and that the successor of the slain king retreated 700 li south to Indrapura, adding that the 982 attack may have struck a minor king of the same dynasty, not Indrapura. The text says only that Le Hoan led armies into northern Champa and leaves out which city was sacked, the retreat and the 1007 envoy's report of a flight to Foshi. The article gives the end of Indrapura as capital as 982 or the 12th century; left out beyond power passing to Vijaya by the 12th century.

Entry says the railway opened near Rio in 1854; the article gives only the start of construction in 1852. Not contradictory; both kept apart. The saved article has no section on his career beyond the lead, so the Career section rests on the lead.

The entry dates his death to c. 675 BCE; the article says Esarhaddon killed him in 676 BCE. The year is left out of the text. The entry places him as ruler of Ishkuza in north-western Iran; the article places the Scythian centre in eastern Transcaucasia (present-day Azerbaijan). The text states the article's account of the Scythian settlement without naming his own seat.

The article contradicts itself on the fall of Žabljak (1477 and 1478) and says in its lead that he lost his realm in 1479; no year given in the text. His two marriages (Voisava Arianiti; Mara, daughter of Stefan Vukčić, in 1469) left out for length.
Short article (about 280 words); two sections only. Entry says Tezozomoc's forces killed him in 1418; the article agrees on 1418 as his death year.
Article mixes the forms Izates and Izina; Izates used throughout.
The article gives no death date; the entry's c. 645 is not contradicted.

The article contradicts itself on when building began: 1551 under Amar Singh (lead and Gul Mahal), about 1616 under Amar Singh (History), and 1560 under Udai Singh II (Geography). The entry says built mainly under Karan Singh II in the 1620s. No start date is given in the text. The article says Shah Jahan lived there in 1623; the entry gives 1623–1624. No year given in the text.

The article dates the founding of the Jalairid Sultanate to 1330 but also places Hasan Buzurg's rise after the death of Arpa Ke'un in 1336; the entry says the 1330s, after the Ilkhanate's collapse. No founding year given in the text. The October 2024 count of people with the clan name in Mongolia left out (an 'as of' figure).

James Wise's figure of seventeen years (1414–31) for the conversions left out; it does not match the reign dates of the entry. The entry says the Eklakhi Mausoleum is probably his tomb; the article says his burial there is disputed. Worded as 'was said to have been buried there, though this is disputed'.

The entry says Aurangzeb added an entrance gateway after his conquest in 1686; the article says he added an eastern doorway and changed the flooring, without a year. The text mentions only the flooring for Aurangzeb, so as not to repeat the entry.
The entry dates completion to around 1470; the article gives 1473. No completion year in the text. The article gives the pishtaq as over 200 feet tall, which seems doubtful; left out.

The article's lead dates the treaties to 1738 (Leeward) and 1739 (Windward), but its body to 1739 and 1740, as the entry does. The text names no year for Cudjoe's treaty and calls the war 'the war of the 1730s' because the article dates the First Maroon War both 1728–1739 and c. 1728–1740.

The article gives Karsé Kongtrül's birth as 1904 and also says he was enthroned at twelve in 1902; years of birth left out. The two rival fourth incarnations (both born 1995, one of whom left monastic life in 2016) left out: living persons.

The article calls Janusz the second son and Stanisław his younger brother, contradicting itself; the entry makes Stanisław the elder. Their order of birth is left out. Jan Długosz died in 1480, before the brothers' deaths; the article attributes the tuberculosis view to him anyway. The view is given without his name.
The article says both that the composition was composed by Guru Angad and is mostly Guru Nanak's, and that it is Guru Nanak's first composition; worded to keep both.

The article's lead says he founded Kapurthala State in 1772, while a later section dates his occupation of Kapurthala to December 1779 (with Rae-ka-kot taken in 1770); the entry says the 1770s. Kapurthala's date left out. Left out the raids freeing captives of Nadir Shah in 1739, told in the article without sources and in a register close to the disputed rescue stories it later questions. The article reports that Ganesh Das Vadehra disputed that the Sikhs minted the Lahore coins; Ghulam Ali Azad corroborates them. Coins not restated beyond Gupta's view, since the entry already gives them.
Desc says Albert recaptured Brandenburg in June 1157; the article gives 11 June 1157: consistent. The article also says it is unclear whether Jaxa was pagan or Christian; left out for length.

The article reports several versions of Jayapala's release by Mahmud (sold in a slave market for 80 dirhams or dinars per Unsuri, Minhaj and Isami; or ransomed for 250,000 dinars and 50 elephants around March 1002, which Rahman prefers), then says the story of his capture and release 'seems doubtful' and gives the pyre story. The entry states capture, abdication and the pyre. Release accounts left out to avoid a contradiction on the page. The article dates the end of his rule to 1001; the entry gives d. 1002. Left as the entry has it; no death year printed.
The entry's 'about a thousand troops' and surrender to Cornwallis are not in the article; not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; it adds only a few lines to the entry (forced labour at Mantasoa, the 1857 coup, his return in 1861, the inheritance dispute)

Left out the present-tense figures (share of FDI and of Dubai's GDP, employment, 'as of 2025' counts) and the claim that it is the US Navy's most visited foreign port: present-day rankings and figures. The article spells the road 'Skiekh Zayed Road'; written Sheikh Zayed Road, as it also appears in the article.
The article lists a Daoist 'Tian Pia' (likely Tian Pian); left out because of the doubtful spelling. The article says some argue the Tao Te Ching was edited there; left out as a weak claim.

The article says he distinguished himself at the conquest of Saint-Quentin in 1583; the date looks doubtful and the event uncertain, so it is left out. The Treaty of Stadtilm (1599), named in the entry, is not in the article.

SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance (mostly a list of children), and it contradicts the entry: it dates his rule from 1355 and the partition to his father's abdication in 1346, against the entry's partition of 1344, and calls the 1366 rank Imperial Count rather than princely count

The entry's visit to Rarotonga in 1823 with Papeiha is not in the article; not repeated. The article's account of the 1827-1828 voyage of the Messenger of Peace (sailing for the Society Islands, then moving the family to Raiatea) is confused; left out beyond the building of the ship.

The article says that on 1 April 1811 he took office as first President of 'the United Provinces of New Granada'; the entry (and the article's own lead) make him President of Cundinamarca. Only Cundinamarca printed.

The entry calls the alliance the League of the Interior; the article the Unitarian League. Written as 'the league'. The article's sentence that Pueyrredón made him colonel in 1814 is doubtful (Pueyrredón became Supreme Director in 1816); left out.
The article dates Hugh Laurie's recording to 2011 in one place and to his 2013 album Let Them Talk in another; no year printed.

The article frames most of his Afghan career as Harlan's own claims; the text hedges the title. The entry's statement that he helped train the Sikh army is not detailed in the article; not repeated. Left out the living descendant who holds the title.

The article says the fort was never taken except for a one-day occupation by Kamran Mirza in 1534, decades before the fort was built (1589); left out. The article dates the Karan Mahal to c. 1680 to mark a victory over Aurangzeb, but gives Karan Singh's reign as 1631–1639; the date is left out. Its date for Rai Singh's Phool Mahal (1571–1668) is also a slip; left out. The article says the fort was renamed in the early 20th century and that Ganga Singh moved to Lalgarh in 1902.

The entry says Dunhuang was flooded; the article speaks only of the slaughter of its people. Flooding not mentioned, no contradiction. His patronage of Buddhism and Dharmakshema are not in the saved text.

The article names the interpreter who wrote the dedication/preface as both Yoshio Kōsaku and Yoshio Kōgyū; left out. The entry credits Sugita, Maeno and colleagues with publication; the article names Sugita as author and Suharaya Ichibee as publisher: no contradiction.

Left out the article's claims that the fort is the largest and oldest in the Himalayas with mentions over 4,000 years. The article describes the fort as 'on the west bank of the Sutlej' in the 1807 siege, which looks like a slip; left out.

The article is written largely from the Armenian side; the text attributes the grievances and the 'national liberation' view to Armenians and leaves out the article's unattributed characterisations of Azerbaijani nationalism. The article contradicts itself on figures: the 20 February 1988 vote was 110-17 in one place, while a 'unanimous vote' in June is also mentioned; crowds of 100,000-300,000 are placed in Stepanakert in one section and in Yerevan in the timeline. Crowd sizes left out. The article places Theater Square's demonstrations in 1988; the 'referendum in 1988' of the lead is not supported elsewhere and is left out.

The entry says the river flows through north-eastern Bangladesh; the article places it in Rajshahi Division (the north-west) and in Rangpur and Bogura. I gave the districts only and no compass direction for Bangladesh. The article spells the map-maker Van Den Brouk and Ven den Brouck; I wrote Van den Brouck.

The entry says hundreds of thousands passed through the camp; the article says over 1,000,000 inmates. I gave no total. The article says the camp operated 1930-1959 in its lead and was established in 1931 in its history; the entry has 1931-1959. I used 1931 only. The article says 'free labor'; rendered as worked without pay. The Zhanalyk executions are in the article's Karlag 'Modern times' section; the article does not say they were Karlag prisoners, and I did not say so.
The article's lists of rulers and family tree are empty in the saved copy.

The article says the Kashag was created in 1721 and set by the Qianlong Emperor in 1751; the entry says formally established in 1751. I kept both as a first creation and a lasting form. The article's list of present ministers left out (no present-day office holders).
Left out the 'Top 100 Castles' and 'Five Greatest Mountain Castles' lists as rankings.

The article says he took the throne in 1510 in one place and ruled from about 1511 in another; the entry has about 1511. I gave no accession year. The article calls Dughlat a 'Kazakh Chagatayid governor'; I wrote only governor of Kashmir. The article's claim that Qasim thereby conquered all of modern Kazakhstan and much of Uzbekistan left out as unsourced-sounding; kept the lands north of the Syr Darya. The death is not told in the article, so the heading is Legacy. The law code's name is already in the entry and not repeated.

The entry says he was captured and killed by Kyrgyz forces; the article says he was killed in battle against Kyrgyz manap chieftains. I wrote that he died at their hands, without saying how. The article lists Bopay both as one of his six children and as his younger sister; left out. The article calls him the last khan of the Kazakh Khanate; not repeated.

The article gives her birth as 1778 in the lead and around 1778 in the text; the entry has c. 1778. No year given in my text. The article says Kamehameha 'usurped' his cousin Kīwalaʻō; I wrote 'overthrown'. The article says she was 11 in 1790, which with a birth around 1778 is consistent; not used.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance beyond the description (location, a quoted excavation report, the scrolls). It also dates the salvage excavation to August-September 1975 and only the scrolls' find to 1979, while the entry says the burial caves were excavated in 1979, so most of what it adds would contradict the entry.

The article calls the kholop a type of feudal serf in Kievan Rus' from the 9th to the early 12th centuries; the entry speaks of the 11th and 12th centuries. I gave neither span. The article writes 'Boevie kholopi'; I used the transliteration boevye kholopy. The ways of becoming a kholop and the 1722-1724 poll tax are already in the entry and not repeated.

Left out the article's paragraph on modern interpretations of Khomeini's rule as drawing on farr (present-day politics). Soudavar's and Granoff's proposals (the winged emblems; Tobatsu Bishamon) left out for length.

The article says only that King Mu was 'possibly' the son of Cheng and Zheng Mao; the entry calls Mu his son. I did not name Mu's mother. The article does not mention the Battle of Chengpu or Cheng's parents, which the entry gives; not repeated.
The article gives his personal name as Xiong Che, also known as Xiong Tong; the entry gives Xiong Tong. I wrote 'also known by the personal name Xiong Che'.

The article says the 2022 research showed the dynasty was an offshoot of Caracol's and that this confirmed the strontium analysis, which points to Tikal; I gave only that the research linked the dynasty to Caracol. The article writes '822 a.C.'; read as 822 CE, consistent with the Classic period.

Left out the article's dating of the Yoga Vasistha passage to 'about 10th century BCE', which is unclear and unsourced, and its racial characterisation ('Mongoloid in appearance'). The article dates Lévi's conclusion to 1985; no year given.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words, and beyond the description it adds only the 1891 laying-out on Klipspruit farm, informal settlements from 1903, a 2005 unemployment figure and renewal plan, popular-culture mentions and a railway station: too little for a longer text.

The article gives the Haleri Rajas as ruling from around 1600 in one place and 1602-1834 in another; I wrote 'from around 1600'. The article says Kodagu is called 'the cradle of Indian hockey' and lists sports people and present-day demands for homeland status; left out (no rankings or present-day politics). The article's etymology section derives the name from koḍa 'western'; the origin section gives mist, hills or west. I gave the origin section's three readings.

The article dates the Chola conquest to the tenth century in its lead and to the 9th century under Aditya I in its history; I gave only Rajaraja I's late-10th-century rule, which both allow. The article dates the fall of the Vijayanagara Empire to 1646; no year given. Left out present-day caste conflicts and the demand for statehood (present-day politics), and the economic figures 'as of 2021-22'.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance (sources near Mount Dena, a list of dams, the Pulvar tributary, the Sivand dam of 2007, a dam of Darius's reign); not enough for 260 words without padding. It does not give the river's length or mention Adud al-Dawla, which the entry has.

The article says the Kedhaton (royal palace) existed on the site in 1509, which conflicts with the late-16th-century founding in both the article and the entry; left out. Left out the Babad Mangkubumi legend of Ratu Kidul to save words.

Entry says the dam supplied the Shivanasamudra power station; the file does not name it, so it is not mentioned. The file contradicts itself on Brindavan Gardens (built by Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar vs planned by Mirza Ismail) and on the automatic gates (Visvesvaraya vs 'Sir Erwin' in 1920); both left out. The file gives the 1932 inauguration; left out to keep to the entry's 1911–1931.
Entry says 'a peasant revolt in 1831'; the file places the outbreak of the Nagar revolt towards the end of the 1820s and the takeover in 1831. Worded without dating the revolt.

The file calls the principal burial a king and the woman 'probably the king's wife or concubine'; the entry says a nobleman and his wife. Worded without either title. The file describes an electrum cup at the woman's feet with scenes from Scythian mythology; the entry speaks of a vase showing Scythian warriors. Probably the same object; left out. The file dates the tomb 400-350 BC, consistent with the entry; not repeated.

Entry traces the Xi through Chinese sources to the Yuwen Xianbei; the file calls them descendants of the Wuhuan who submitted to the Yuwen Xianbei. Worded through the named Chinese histories without choosing. The file says the Xi were 'completely assimilated' into the Liao in 907; the entry has them absorbed from the 10th century as a distinct part of Liao army and administration. Worded as the Khitans absorbing the remnants and founding the Liao in 907, without 'completely assimilated'.

The file dates the annexation of the Kumul Khanate to 1930; the entry does not date it, so the year is left out to avoid implying a different sequence. The file calls the Khotan rising separate; the entry says the revolt helped to spark the First East Turkestan Republic. Worded as a separate rising, without saying it was unconnected.

The file gives the usual day of the celebration as 12 December in its lead and 11 December later; the day is left out. The claim that the defenders' tactics followed the League of Lezha was left out as doubtful and unrelated.
The entry's Mycenaean kingdom of Menelaus is not in the file and is not repeated. Weather records left out.

The file gives his voivodeship as 1295–1314 or 1315 and his death as probably at the end of 1314 or the beginning of 1315 (before 13 May 1315); the entry has from about 1294 and death in 1315. The start of his office and the exact time of death are left out.

The file gives his reign as 1178–1206 without 'c.'; the entry's hedge is kept by not repeating the dates. The file says he withdrew to south-eastern Bengal; the entry says eastern. The date of the Nadia raid is not given in the file and is left out.

The file calls it the world's largest private residence; the entry says among the largest ever built. Not repeated. The file says the palace was constructed in 1890 by Charles Mant and Robert Chisholm; not repeated.
The file's sentence about an examination scandal involving his son Lê Quý Kiêt is garbled and left out.
The file gives the death date as 28 August 1442 in the lead and the visit as 4 August; the entry gives only the year. Not a contradiction; the death day is left out to avoid confusion.

The file dates the Musso War to 1520; left undated as doubtful. The file ends the league with the Napoleonic dissolution and absorption into the Helvetic Republic; the entry's 1799 French invasion is consistent and not repeated.

CONFLICT: the entry says the castle was built by the O'Carrolls of Ely, probably in the 15th century; the file says it was built by the O'Bannon clan, most likely around 1250 (accounts ranging from the 13th to the late 15th century). Builder and date left out. The entry's pass between Ely O'Carroll and Munster is not in the file and not repeated.

The file gives 7,000 French troops in its lead and 6,000 soldiers for the expedition later; no number is used. The file says Toussaint 'arranged for Sonthonax to leave Saint-Domingue as one of its elected representatives in 1797'; the entry has him sent back to France in 1797, consistent.

The file says Rhodes was already held by an independent ruler at the time of the Fourth Crusade (1203–04), usually identified with Leo, possibly with an unknown predecessor; the entry says he seized Rhodes after the Crusade broke up the empire in 1204. The timing of his seizure is left out. The file places his death in the early 1240s; the entry says around 1240. The decade is left out.
Short article; written at the lower length. 'Possibly Ithaca' hedged as the file hedges.

CONFLICT: the entry says Leptis was seized from Carthage by Masinissa around 161 BCE; the file says Masinissa overran Emporia after 201 BCE but that Leptis itself remained unconquered. The Numidian episode is left out. The file spells the modern town Lemta, the entry Lamta; the modern name is not repeated.
The file gives his birth as c. 1292, the entry c. 1290; the birth year is left out. Short article; written at the lower length.
The article's list of titles gives title 3 as 'about the sexes and their penance', while its description of Title III says it names the noble families; the text follows the description.

The article's lead dates the Old Welsh marginalia to the early part of the 8th century, its Marginalia section dates the first two inscriptions to the mid-9th century; the text follows the section, which agrees with the entry's 9th century at Llandeilo Fawr.

The article's lead says the song was written in the early 1950s, its History section that it was written in 1949 and first performed in 1950 (as the entry has it); the text gives 1949, as the entry does.
The entry calls Limyra the capital of Pericles; the article says he adopted it as capital of the Lycian League. The text does not repeat either.
The entry's seizure of Klaipėda in 1923 is not in the article and is not repeated.
The article tells almost nothing of the governorship itself; the text gives his family and offices at home.
The entry says the MacDermots of Moylurg gave their name to the Annals of Loch Cé; the article does not mention the MacDermots, so the text says nothing of them.
The entry spells the island Inisfallen, the article Innisfallen.
The article says Delgrès was left with roughly 1000 men and some women before Matouba; the entry speaks of several hundred followers dying with him. The text gives no number.
The article does not name the Rebellion Losses Bill; it describes the amnesty bill and the burning of the Parliament without a year. The text keeps to the article's wording.
The article names the fort Aduatuca; the entry spells it Atuatuca. The text does not name it.
The article calls the cathedral Neo-Gothic; the text does not repeat the word for a building of his time.

The article's lead gives his birth as 29 July 1832, the Medal of Honor citation 29 June 1832; no day is given. The article dates the Metropolitan's purchase of the collection to 1872, while the entry has him digging until 1876; the year of purchase is left out. The article says the consulship lasted to 1877, the entry that he dug until 1876; the text gives no end year.

The entry counts the Lango among the Luo; the article names the Lango as Highland Nilotes and rivals of the Joluo. The Lango are left out of the text. The article dates the southward migration of the Southern Luo to the early centuries of the second millennium, about eight hundred years ago; the entry has the spread from around the fifteenth century. No date of the first migration is given.

The entry says Ma Yin was from Xuzhou; the article says Yanling, in modern Xuchang (Xuzhou is the old name of the prefecture of Xuchang), so the text names Yanling and modern Xuchang only. The entry's tea trade is not in the excerpt; the text mentions only the coinage and silk policies the article gives.
The article has no history of the region beyond the 1934 soil rating; the entry's 19th-century sugar refining is not in it.
The closing judgement about the town's destruction is attributed to Maspero, as the article gives it in the paragraph citing him.

The article dates his reign 590–630; the entry has c. 600–630, so no starting year is given. The article states the conversion by Appar as fact; the entry hedges it as tradition, so the text keeps the entry's hedge. The article's claims that he built the Mamallapuram lighthouse and a 'Kanchi University' were left out as doubtful.
The article's lead says he ascended in 1435, its body 14 May 1436; the entry has 1436, which the text follows.

The article says Thembuland was annexed shortly after the death of King Sarhili, while the entry says by 1885; no date is given. The present king, Buyelekhaya Dalindyebo, is living, and his convictions and disputes were left out.
Restorations by the Archaeological Survey of India, criticised for replacing mud and stone courtyards with granite, were left out as ongoing.

The article's genetic claims (archaic introgression, Mursi-related ancestry, haplogroups carried to the Americas) and its lists of present-day people of Tikar descent were left out. It gives Wou-Ten a reign of 1201 to 1246, which sits oddly with Tikar kingdoms founded in the late 14th century; the years are left out.
The entry speaks of pay far below that of French soldiers; the article speaks of unequal pensions and unpaid arrears, so the text keeps to those.
The article lists the five cantons' allies and the neutral cantons in more detail than given here.

The article's Legacy section offers an unsourced theory that the surviving Qasar clan gave its name to the Hazaras; left out. The family list dates him as Ilkhan 1338–1339, while the text says he was recognised from 1335–1336 by the east and by Ḥasan Buzurg in 1339 and 1340–1344; no reign years given.
